title: US arrests: the machine peaked in 1997
unit: Estimated arrests per year, millions (FBI; excludes traffic)
note: US arrests peaked in 1997 at 15.28 million — a fact most readers do not know — and 2024 is 51% below that. Drug arrests peaked separately in 2006 (1.89M) and remain the largest single category. Constant across the whole era: 82–84% of all arrests are for lesser, non-index offences. Sparse points are drawn as points, not smoothed into a line the data cannot support; dotted stretches are years that are not Tier A. The sweeping operations in the register above — the World Cup's 905 arrests against HSI's 2,545 for all of FY2024 — sit inside these annual millions, which is the scale a headline arrest number should be read against.
publisher: FBI CIUS/CDE; Council on Criminal Justice corroborating

series.name: All arrests
series.basis_short: FBI estimated arrests, all offences, excluding traffic
caveats: Selected years, not a continuous annual series — the FBI's own estimates for the years shown, one consistent series (never mixed with the BJS 1980-2009 series, which uses different weights and yields ~11.6M for 1997).
2016 and 2021 are known national data gaps and are not shown.
An arrest is an enforcement action, not a conviction; 82-84% of arrests across this whole period are for lesser (Part II) offences.
series.unit: estimated criminal arrests per calendar year

series.name: Drug arrests
caveats: Peaked in 2006 at 1,889,810; 2024 (822,488) is still the largest single arrest category.
1980 and 2006-2008 values corroborated via compilations of FBI Table 29 (Tier B where marked).
series.unit: estimated drug-abuse violation arrests per calendar year

series.name: Civil immigration arrests (ICE)
series.basis_short: ICE ERO administrative arrests — civil immigration violations, federal fiscal year
series.publisher: DHS OHSS annual flow reports (FY2011-2020); ICE annual reports (FY2021-2024)
series.unit: administrative arrests per federal fiscal year (Oct-Sep)
caveats: CIVIL arrests under immigration law, adjudicated by immigration judges — a separate legal system from the criminal arrests on the other two lines.
Federal FISCAL years (October-September), plotted at the fiscal-year label; the criminal series are calendar years.
The all-time peak is FY2011 (322,093) — the Secure Communities era, when most arrests were custodial transfers from jails, not street operations.
FY2022 and FY2023 are inflated by ICE processing border-encounter backlogs in the interior; ICE itself says so. They overstate interior enforcement.
FY2015 and FY2022 carry small official revisions (117,983 vs 119,772; 142,750 restated 142,873).

NO official FY2025 or FY2026 total exists — DHS stopped publishing detailed enforcement tables after November 2024. The 2025-26 surge is documented only through FOIA'd ICE records: 95,629 arrests Jan 20-Jun 10 2025, roughly 217,500 Jan 20-Oct 15 2025, and a rate 4.4x the late-Biden baseline by January 2026 (street arrests up 11x). This line therefore ENDS at FY2024 not because the surge is small but because no official number exists yet.
Even the FY2011 peak equals roughly 2-3% of the same year's criminal arrests — the vertical gap between this line and the others is the scale of the two systems.

themes.statement: Criminal arrests peaked in 1997 at 15.3 million. 2024, at 7.5 million, is 51% below that.
Yes, 15.3 million is real — but an arrest is an event, not a person. One person arrested three times counts three times.
Most arrests never become imprisonment: 7.5 million criminal arrests a year sit alongside 7.9 million jail admissions.
On any given day 657,500 people are in jail — 69% not yet convicted — and 1.25 million are in prison.
Is the system overcrowded? The federal government stopped counting in 2016.
That year the US stood at 114% of its lowest reported prison capacity, with 26 states over 100%. No edition since carries the table.
Jails run the other way — 73% of rated capacity in 2023 — though 12% of individual jurisdictions were over their own.
The strain the record does show is in immigration detention: above 70,000 held in January 2026, against 41,500 funded beds.
Civil immigration arrests are the near-floor line, and that is the point. Even its FY2011 peak of 322,093 is about 2–3% of criminal arrest volume.
It ends at FY2024 because no official 2025–26 total exists. The surge is documented only through FOIA'd records.
Of 33 federal defendants charged with non-immigration crimes in Chicago's Operation Midway Blitz, 25 were cleared, against 2 guilty pleas.

accuracy_note: About the accuracy of these figures: arrest totals are estimates assembled from agency reports, and two official federal criminal-arrest series disagree (see the data-quality register); 2016 and 2021 are national gaps. The immigration line is federal FISCAL years and ends at FY2024 — DHS stopped publishing detailed enforcement tables after November 2024, so the 2025-26 surge exists only in FOIA'd records. An arrest, in either system, is an event — not a person, and not a conviction.
